A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GSI research, with matching authors, core algorithm, models, and original benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching the relocated proofs and code disclosure.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy experiments on three reasoning benchmarks, runtime and acceptance measurements, and a rejection-step ablation in Tables 1–2 and Figure 2.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on five benchmarks, runtime measurements, parameter sweeps, and reasoning-trace analyses in Section 5 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: Both versions use draft sampling, reward-plus-log-likelihood weighting, soft selection, threshold rejection, and target-model S-BoN fallback. Algorithm 1 in v2 clarifies history conditioning and sample indices; the PDFs do not establish a new method component or changed inference procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM while retaining MATH500, OlympiadBench, and Minerva Math. This broadens coverage to grade-school word problems and STEM multiple-choice questions, including biology examples in Appendix B.5.

E2.justification: The main implemented baselines remain RSD and small/base-model S-BoN. v2 Figure 2 adds RSD and small-model S-BoN to the corresponding scaling/rejection comparison. Section 5.1 also introduces a quantitative SPECS comparison using published scores, explicitly without running SPECS and with different evaluation subsets.

E3.justification: Appendices B.2–B.3 add systematic MATH500 protocols sweeping beta from 0 to 1000 and rejection thresholds from 0.05 to 1.5 across n=1,4,16,64,256, including accuracy–latency and Pareto comparisons. The default models and decoding hyperparameters remain unchanged. v2's newly specified subset sizes do not establish that v1 used different subsets.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the rejection-step ablation, v2 adds acceptance-rate scaling, beta and threshold sensitivity studies, and a threshold Pareto analysis. Section 5.2 and Appendix B.5 introduce paired GSI/RSD reasoning cases examining error correction, rejection of correct steps, and failures where GSI loses or both methods fail.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over two random seeds without confidence intervals. v2 reports three seeds and introduces 95% confidence intervals in accuracy and runtime tables and several figures. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, although the interval-construction procedure is not specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark, sensitivity, and case-study results and revises existing estimates. In Table 1, Minerva accuracy at n=16 changes from 29.6% to 28.2% for GSI and from 36.0% to 33.6% for target S-BoN. Runtime averages also change, but aggregate five rather than three datasets; these replacements do not establish same-setting speedups.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 retains its substantive bound. For Theorem 2, v2 Appendix A.2 introduces Assumption 2 concerning golden rewards on the acceptance set and the target distribution's probability of that set. It revises the rejection-mixture decomposition, adds a third proof term and bounding argument, and adds an asymptotic remark relaxing one condition. These materially revise v1 Appendix B's reward guarantee.

C1.justification: The central GSI contribution remains intact. v2 explicitly claims priority as the first test-time scaling method with guarantees to the optimal tilted distribution and extends its superiority claims to SPECS. Expected-reward approximation is promoted into the abstract but was already claimed in v1; its theorem now carries additional assumptions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of how beta balances reward and likelihood, why threshold choice depends on n, and how tilted rewards can reject correct reasoning or miss errors. It also discusses weak STEM generations, selection of short illustrative traces, runtime sensitivity to batching, and the limited comparability of SPECS scores.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the double-newline step delimiter, dataset subset sizes, full-batch timing, additional A100/H200 usage, software libraries, and RewardHub/prm800k answer grading. These refine reproducibility information. Model identities, principal decoding settings, H100 timing hardware, and the public code URL were already disclosed in v1.

R1.justification: v2 expands research positioning through a dedicated related-work discussion of parallel versus sequential scaling and a substantive comparison with concurrent SPECS, including contrasting theoretical assumptions. It also adds relevant work on self-consistency, introspection, data-constrained scaling, and smoothed best-of-n analysis.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and contribution narrative, separates related work from background, expands reward-model and method explanations, and reorganizes the appendices. New experiment subsections and a contents page improve navigation; the changes extend beyond inserting additional scientific results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with colored components and explicit acceptance/fallback branches. Figure 2 becomes a six-panel display with additional comparators and uncertainty bands. Tables are reorganized by n, and v2 adds sensitivity plots, a Pareto figure, an extended runtime table, and colored reasoning-trace boxes marking rejected steps.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's sparse empirical validation through broader task coverage, uncertainty reporting, parameter sensitivity and latency analyses, and concrete success and failure traces. These additions make the method's tradeoffs and limitations much easier to assess. The revised theorem states additional assumptions explicitly. Although the stronger SPECS superiority claim remains limited by unmatched evaluation subsets, the empirical and explanatory gains provide a clear overall improvement.
